title: Johnstown Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Johnstown wells are typically 29 feet deep, with finished-well costs commonly modeled at $7,400-$14,000.
h1: Johnstown, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html: This page covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Johnstown in Weld County. The records show a shallow plains setting overall, but the local well file includes different aquifers, uses, construction dates, and levels of reporting. Of 1,313 wells in the Colorado DWR permit records, 683 are recorded as constructed. Only 795 report a total depth, 84 report a pump yield, and 165 report a static water level. That matters when comparing a property: the statistics describe the reported wells, not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Johnstown?
sections.html:
Johnstown’s reported wells are shallow by Colorado standards. The median total depth is 29 feet, and the middle half runs from 18 to 40 feet. The 90th percentile is 60 feet, while the deepest recorded well reaches 1,000 feet.

That range should shape a drilling bid, but it should not be treated as a promised depth. 95% of wells in the depth mix are under 100 feet; 2% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 3% are between 300 and 600 feet. Permits name Denver Basin aquifer wells for 55% of the records, along with alluvial and unnamed or fractured-bedrock entries. The lot’s exact geology and intended use still control the final design.

sections.heading: Expected well yield near Johnstown
sections.html:
The reported yield numbers are strong overall, but the sample is limited to 84 wells. The median pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half spans 15.0 to 400.0 gallons per minute. That wide upper range means the records include some unusually productive wells and should not be read as a standard output for every parcel.

79% of the reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 18% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 4% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute. For a buyer, confirm the permitted use, storage, pump test, and any household demand before relying on a neighboring yield.

sections.heading: Johnstown water levels and recent measurements
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are close to the surface. The median depth to water is 10 feet, with the middle half between 6 and 14 feet. That is useful for estimating casing, trenching, and pump conditions, but a static level can change with season, pumping, recharge, and nearby construction.

The decade comparison does not show a dropping table in these records. The median measurement was 14 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 9 feet below the surface in the 2020s, meaning the later reported measurements were shallower. The comparison is based on only 165 wells with a static water-level report, so it is a local record trend rather than a guarantee for a particular site near Milliken, Berthoud, or Johnstown.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Johnstown, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity is not limited to recent development. The records show permits from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2026. The largest decade is the 2020s, with 366 permits. The 1990s account for 184, the 2000s for 146, and the 2010s for 123. Earlier decades include 37 permits in the 1950s, 43 in the 1960s, 31 in the 1970s, and 39 in the 1980s.

The most active names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 449 wells, followed by Kelley Dewatering And Construction Company (Creech, Jason) and Clement, Glenn A., with 57 each. These are permit-record names, not a recommendation. Verify current licensing, insurance, references, and the exact scope of a bid.

sections.heading: What a new Johnstown well may cost
sections.html:
The cost model for Johnstown assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a typical drilling rate of $50-$70 per foot. At the local median depth of 29 feet, the drilled hole models to about $1,400-$2,000. That is only the hole, not a functioning water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at approximately $7,400-$14,000 at the median depth. Actual bids can change with access, casing and grout requirements, site distance, electrical service, water treatment, and the well’s permitted use. Ask the driller to separate drilling, casing, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and restoration so competing bids cover the same work.

sections.heading: Johnstown risks: water quality, low yield, and septic
sections.html:
Shallow water is convenient but deserves careful protection. The mapped area within about 10 miles contains 1,599 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 2 historic mine features. These mapped sites do not prove contamination at a specific parcel. They do justify checking the property’s location, testing existing water, and asking the county or Colorado DWR about any relevant records.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even where nearby wells perform well. A shallow well also needs proper casing and grout, separation from septic components, and a design suited to flooding, drainage, and the building footprint. Confirm septic setbacks and soil suitability before choosing a house site. Water quality testing should match the local risk review and the intended household use.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Johnstown: a practical check
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit file for the exact parcel, then compare nearby wells in Johnstown, Milliken, Berthoud, and the surrounding Weld County area. Look for construction depth, aquifer description, permitted use, yield, static level, and whether the record shows a completed well. The local database is helpful, but reporting is incomplete: only 84 wells report yield and 165 report static water level.

Before closing, make the well permit, water-use rights, pump test, laboratory water test, and septic approval part of the due diligence list. For a new build, obtain a site-specific drilling and pump quote before finalizing the house location. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask whether an augmentation plan or other water-right requirement applies. The permit’s authorized use matters as much as the well’s depth.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Johnstown, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Johnstown is 29 feet. The middle half runs from 18 to 40 feet, and 95% of the depth-mix records are under 100 feet. The database also includes wells as deep as 1,000 feet, so a nearby shallow well does not guarantee the same depth on a new parcel.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Johnstown?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50-$70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 29-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $1,400-$2,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $7,400-$14,000. Access, casing, grout, electrical distance, testing, and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Johnstown wells produce?
faq.a: Among 84 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 15.0 to 400.0 gallons per minute, and 79% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Those figures are not a guarantee for a new well. Confirm the permit, pump test, storage, and intended household demand for the specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Johnstown?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that a particular well is safe to drink. There are 1,599 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove contamination at a parcel, but a buyer should test existing well water and review nearby environmental records before relying on it.

faq.q: Is Johnstown well water table going down?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a declining water table. Median depth to water was 14 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 9 feet in the 2020s, so the later reported measurements were shallower. Only 165 wells report static water level, however. Seasonal pumping and individual site conditions still make a current measurement important.
